definition: Available only in small amounts, so there is not enough to meet the need for it.
example: Fresh water becomes scarce on the island during the long dry season.
nuance: Scarce means there is not enough of something people need or want; rare just means uncommon, whether or not anyone wants it.
prompt: A small town's only bakery struggles after a winter storm blocks deliveries.
options: With roads closed for days, flour grew scarce and the bakery cut its hours.
The flour was so scarce that bags were stacked to the ceiling of the storeroom.
The baker felt scarce when the wind rattled the windows all night long.
To stretch their supply, the bakers scarce the flour by mixing in extra water.
reasons: Blocked deliveries left too little flour to meet demand, so the word fits.
A storeroom piled high describes plenty, the reverse of a shortage.
This confuses the word with the look-alike scared; it describes supply, not fear.
The word is an adjective, not a verb meaning to ration or thin something out.

practice.prompt: Volunteers plan a summer hike through a dry desert canyon.
options: Shade is scarce on the trail, so hikers can rest beneath its many leafy trees.
The canyon trail was so scarce that finishing it took nearly eight hours.
One volunteer is scarce of heights and will wait near the trailhead.
Because shade is scarce along the trail, the leaders set the start time for dawn.
reasons: Many trees would provide plenty of shade, which contradicts the word.
The word describes a limited quantity of something, not a route's length or difficulty.
This mixes the word up with scared; being afraid has nothing to do with short supply.
Little shade means hikers need to avoid the midday sun, a sensible response to a shortage.
